Title: Modulo
Pitch_Text:
Dive into the world of Sylva and become the last bastion of the Automatons. Place defensive towers and upgrade them using specialized modules to repel the invasion of the “Acris,” a mysterious threat.

Modulo is a 2D Tower Defense game with a top-down camera, mixed with Base Defender mechanics. Its game design emphasizes adaptability, reactivity, and strategic planning of your defenses. A key feature of Modulo is the creation of paths tailored to each enemy’s specific behavior.
SumUp_Text:
Modulo is a project in which I learned how to prioritize tasks and efficiently manage scope within a limited timeframe.

It was also a first introduction to several fundamental concepts for clean code architecture, such as polymorphism, the basics of optimization, and the use of Managers.

Project carried out as part of my studies at Rubika Valenciennes.
Realisation_Text:
Being mostly the only programmer on the team, I handled all aspects of programming while also taking on the role of game designer for this project. Here are the key elements of the project:

• Enemies: To encourage adaptability, Modulo featured six enemy types with varied behaviors, such as the “Mage,” who boosted nearby enemies, or the “Stunner,” who paralyzed the player’s defenses. Through this system, I discovered the basics of inheritance-based polymorphism, making the code more readable and easier to modify throughout production.

• Pathfinding: In line with the enemy diversity, multiple pathfinding systems were implemented. The “Breaker,” for example, prioritized destroying buildings, while the “Sprinter” avoided them. Pathfinding was first implemented using Dijkstra’s algorithm and later replaced by A* for optimization reasons. Elements such as “path beacons” allowed us to dynamically influence enemy trajectories by attracting them to specific locations.

• Wave system: To provide a long-term experience, I designed a system of infinitely extendable waves. Enemies are generated using mathematical formulas defining the proportion of each enemy type in a given wave, as well as their total number. A preview of the next wave was integrated into the interface, allowing the player to anticipate its composition.

• Towers and upgrades: Towers can be upgraded using specialized modules, such as the “Fire” module dealing area damage or the “Ice” module slowing enemies. These modules are physically present on the map, making them vulnerable to enemy attacks. A single module can enhance up to eight nearby towers.

• Optimization: Due to the game’s infinite nature, optimization was a major challenge during production. Special care was taken to limit the use of Update() or other performance-costly functions, favoring coroutines and an event-based system instead.
Amelioration_Text:
Although polymorphism was used for some aspects of the game, it could have been leveraged more extensively, particularly for the module system, which could have derived from a “Module” class with a polymorphic “UpgradeTower()” method. The concept of abstract classes was still unknown to me at the time, but it could have contributed to a more modular architecture. Optimization could also have been improved, as the game still suffered from slowdowns, especially due to enemy pathfinding algorithms. Finally, some scripts remained somewhat long and difficult to read, although a clear improvement had been made compared to the previous project (Withering Depths).

Nevertheless, this project allowed me to learn how to make more modular and adaptive code while touching on optimization challenges.
